newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Stark choice in Albania poll - ballots or bullets?.
newsitem.headline: Stark choice in Albania poll - ballots or bullets?.

text.p: Albania, armed to the teeth with looted weapons, has just four weeks to prepare for early elections that could make the difference between anarchy and stability.
The international community is trying to help Europe's poorest country to patch its political system back together, but grave security concerns overshadow the June 29 polls.

An estimated one million weapons -- no one can say for sure how many -- were plundered from armouries during riots in March after thousands of people lost their savings in the collapse of shady pyramid investment schemes.

Every night, when a 9 p.m. curfew passes, the firing starts. Round after round from Kalashnikovs, pistols, and even heavy machineguns, pierce the night air -- some fired to ward off criminals, others out of boredom.

"I think the only really important thing in terms of certifying freeness and fairness (of the elections) is: do Albanian voters feel safe and secure enough to cast their ballots?" a Western diplomat said.
In many parts of this former communist country of 3.4 million, both election candidates and OSCE observers are potentially at risk.

In the southern port city of Vlore, where the riots first flared, residents have made it clear that right-wing President Sali Berisha is not welcome. "If he came it would be cause for war," a local businessman said.
Herbert Grubmayr of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) told Reuters: "We cannot say so far which parts of the territory of Albania we can really reach.
"The security situation is very volatile. One day it might be safe and another day not, so we will have to go by trial and error procedures."
The March riots, in which several hundred people were killed, forced Berisha to form a national unity government and agree to early elections.
But parties opposing him fear a repeat of the May 1996 elections, condemned as seriously flawed by the United States and OSCE.
The Socialists, powerful Berisha rivals who pulled out of the 1996 vote saying it was rigged, demand the state of emergency be lifted to prevent ballot-stuffing after curfew.

The OSCE will send 400 short-term observers, plus technical experts and other advisers, to monitor the vote. It will appoint an internationally respected overseer to say whether the elections were free and fair.
But no one, not even the 6,000-strong Italian-led multi-national military force (MMF) sent here in April primarily to protect aid supplies, is trying to get the stolen weapons back.

"The MMF are not police, but they will, for election purposes, help to ascertain conditions which would make it possible to hold elections," said Grubmayr, resident deputy to OSCE Albania envoy Franz Vranitzky.

"They will not police the country, this is outside their mandate, but they are...instructed to look out for the safety of the members of international organisations, and our teams are certainly members of international organisations."
Grubmayr was adamant that it was up to Albanians to run the elections, and to devise strategies for campaigning in areas where candidates of one party or another are not welcome.
"It cannot be an election which is only held partially in some so-called safe places," he said.
Weeks of delay before the Albanian parties agreed to hold the elections did not make organising them any easier.

The technical experts working for the OSCE in a cramped headquarters in the capital, Tirana, say they face enormous time pressure to obtain 200 vehicles for observers, print ballots, obtain ballot boxes and prod Albanians to compile new voter lists, many of which were destroyed in the riots.

"I was in Albania last year for the May elections and last year there wasn't machine-gun fire in the night, and the registration lists existed," said Lars Bjorklund, a technical expert from the Swedish town of Skelleftea.
"What we have here is a timetable that is very narrow."
"We're not talking about perfect elections," another diplomat said. "We're talking about reasonably acceptable elections and that doesn't seem out of reach.
"But we are sure that perfect elections cannot be held in Albania."
